title: Electromotive Force of a Source, Internal Resistance
topicTitle: Electromotive force of a source, internal resistance
notes: EMF Definition: Electromotive force (EMF, $\mathcal{E}$) is the energy supplied by a source per unit charge to move charge through the complete circuit. It is NOT a force but a potential difference measured in volts. $\mathcal{E} = W/q$ where $W$ is work done by the source and $q$ is charge moved.

Terminal Potential Difference: When current $I$ flows, the terminal voltage $V$ across the source terminals is $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$, where $r$ is internal resistance. The voltage drop $Ir$ inside the source is called lost volts.

Internal Resistance: Every real source (cell, battery, generator) has internal resistance $r$ due to electrolyte resistance, electrode resistance, and chemical factors. It causes the terminal voltage to drop below EMF when current is drawn.
Open Circuit: When $I = 0$ (open circuit), $V = \mathcal{E}$ — the terminal voltage equals the EMF since there is no internal voltage drop.
Short Circuit: When terminals are shorted ($R = 0$), $I = \mathcal{E}/r$ — maximum current flows, limited only by internal resistance. This can damage the source.

Cells in Series: For $n$ identical cells each of EMF $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance $r$ in series: total EMF $= n\mathcal{E}$, total internal resistance $= nr$, equivalent $V = n\mathcal{E} - Inr$.

Cells in Parallel: For $n$ identical cells each of EMF $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance $r$ in parallel: equivalent EMF $= \mathcal{E}$, equivalent internal resistance $= r/n$ (current capacity increases).
Mixed Grouping: Cells in series-parallel combinations balance voltage and current requirements for specific applications.

Determination of EMF and Internal Resistance: Measure terminal voltage $V$ for different currents $I$. Plot $V$ vs $I$: y-intercept $= \mathcal{E}$, slope $= -r$. Alternatively use a potentiometer for accurate EMF measurement.
Power Delivered: Power delivered to external load $R$ is $P = I^2R = (\mathcal{E}/(R+r))^2 R$. Maximum power transfer occurs when $R = r$, with $P_\text{max} = \mathcal{E}^2/4r$.
specificConditions: EMF vs Terminal Voltage: EMF $\mathcal{E}$ is the open-circuit terminal voltage ($I=0$). Terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ drops as current increases due to internal resistance.
Internal Resistance Effects: Internal resistance causes voltage drop ($Ir$), power loss ($I^2r$), and heating inside the source. It limits maximum deliverable current and power.

Maximum Power Transfer: Maximum power is delivered to load when load resistance equals internal resistance ($R = r$). This is important for matching circuits but not for efficiency (efficiency is only 50% at this point).
keyPoints: EMF is energy per unit charge supplied by the source; measured in volts.
Terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$; internal drop $Ir$ is called lost volts.
Cells in series add EMF and internal resistance; parallel cells reduce effective internal resistance.
Maximum power transfer when external resistance equals internal resistance ($R = r$).
importantNotes: EMF is measured in open circuit ($I=0$); terminal voltage is measured under load ($I \neq 0$).
Internal resistance increases as a cell ages or discharges — old batteries have higher $r$ and lower terminal voltage under load.
Short-circuit current $I = \mathcal{E}/r$ can be very large and damage the source — never short a battery.
EMF is not a force despite the name — it is energy per unit charge (volts).
examShortTricks: Open circuit: terminal voltage = EMF. Closed circuit: terminal voltage = EMF - Ir.
Series cells: EMFs add, internal resistances add. Parallel cells: EMF same, internal resistance divides.
Max power transfer: load R = internal r. Efficiency at max power = 50%.
Plot V vs I: y-intercept = EMF, slope magnitude = internal resistance r.
examNotes: NEB frequently asks to derive $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ and explain internal resistance effects.
Numericals on cells in series/parallel are common — calculate equivalent EMF and internal resistance.
Maximum power transfer condition ($R = r$) is a favourite conceptual question.
Potentiometer method for measuring EMF accurately (no current drawn from cell).
examples: A cell has EMF $1.5\text{ V}$ and internal resistance $0.5\,\Omega$. Connected to a $4\,\Omega$ resistor: $I = 1.5/(4+0.5) = 0.333\text{ A}$, terminal $V = 1.5 - 0.333\times0.5 = 1.33\text{ V}$. Lost volts = $0.17\text{ V}$.
Three cells of EMF $2\text{ V}$ each and $r = 0.2\,\Omega$ each in series: $\mathcal{E}_\text{total} = 6\text{ V}$, $r_\text{total} = 0.6\,\Omega$.
Three identical cells ($\mathcal{E} = 1.5\text{ V}$, $r = 0.3\,\Omega$) in parallel: $\mathcal{E}_\text{eq} = 1.5\text{ V}$, $r_\text{eq} = 0.1\,\Omega$.
A battery of EMF $12\text{ V}$ and $r = 0.5\,\Omega$ delivers max power when $R = 0.5\,\Omega$. $P_\text{max} = 12^2/(4\times0.5) = 72\text{ W}$.
practiceQuestions: Q2. Derive the relation $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ for a cell supplying current to an external circuit.
Q3. Three cells each of EMF $2\text{ V}$ and internal resistance $0.5\,\Omega$ are connected in series. Find equivalent EMF and internal resistance.
Q4. Three identical cells of EMF $1.5\text{ V}$ and $r = 0.3\,\Omega$ are connected in parallel. Find equivalent EMF and internal resistance.
Q5. A battery of EMF $10\text{ V}$ and $r = 1\,\Omega$ is connected to $R = 9\,\Omega$. Find current, terminal voltage, and power delivered.
Q6. State the condition for maximum power transfer and find max power for $\mathcal{E} = 12\text{ V}$, $r = 2\,\Omega$.
Q7. How would you determine EMF and internal resistance of a cell experimentally?
practice: Calculate terminal voltage for given EMF, internal resistance, and load current.
Determine equivalent EMF and internal resistance for series/parallel cell combinations.
Apply maximum power transfer condition ($R = r$) to circuit problems.
Use V-I graph method to find EMF (intercept) and internal resistance (slope).
Compute power delivered to load and power wasted in internal resistance.
Solve problems involving mixed series-parallel cell groupings.
universalFacts: EMF is not a force — despite the name, it is energy supplied per unit charge (volts).
A real cell's internal resistance increases as it discharges — old batteries sag under load.
Maximum power transfer occurs at $R = r$ but efficiency is only 50% — for efficiency, use $R \gg r$.
The potential difference across a cell being charged is $V = \mathcal{E} + Ir$ (charging current adds to EMF).
Potentiometer measures true EMF because it draws no current from the cell at balance point.
confusion: Confusing EMF with terminal voltage: EMF is open-circuit voltage; terminal voltage drops under load due to $Ir$.
Thinking EMF is a force: EMF is energy per unit charge (volts), not a mechanical force.
Believing parallel cells add EMF: Parallel identical cells have same EMF as one cell; only current capacity increases.
Assuming max power = max efficiency: At $R = r$, power is max but efficiency is only 50%.
Ignoring internal resistance: Real sources always have internal resistance affecting terminal voltage.

mcs.question: The terminal voltage of a cell supplying current is:
mcs.explanation: $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$, so terminal voltage is less than EMF when current flows.

mcs.question: Internal resistance of a cell causes:
mcs.explanation: Internal resistance causes voltage drop $Ir$, reducing terminal voltage below EMF.

mcs.question: Cells in parallel have equivalent:
options: EMF same, r divided by n
EMF divided by n, r same
EMF same, r multiplied by n

mcs.question: Maximum power is delivered to load when:
mcs.explanation: Maximum power transfer theorem: $R = r$ for max power to load.

summary: EMF is the energy supplied per unit charge by a source; terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ drops due to internal resistance. Cells in series add EMF and internal resistance; parallel cells keep EMF same but divide internal resistance. Maximum power transfer occurs when load resistance equals internal resistance.
